title: Two bottles of water: classifiers
title_target: น้ำสองขวด — Náam sǎawng khùat
goal: Master the part of Thai that trips up almost every Western learner but is simpler than it looks: classifiers — and the "noun, number, classifier" order that never changes.
bekal: state quantities of things in the right order
use the ten most common classifiers
point to a specific item: เสื้อตัวนี้, คนนั้น
get unstuck when you forget a classifier

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — At a convenience store, before catching a train
dialogs.intro: Budi is shopping for a trip. Notice one pattern that repeats six times in this dialogue: the thing first, then the number, and the classifier last. That order never changes.

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [ขอ|Khǎaw][น้ำ|náam][สอง|sǎawng][ขวด|khùat][ครับ|khráp]

lines.speaker: พนักงาน:
lines.text: [ขวด|Khùat][ใหญ่|yài][หรือ|rǔue][ขวด|khùat][เล็ก|lék][คะ|khá]

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [ขวด|Khùat][ใหญ่|yài][ครับ|khráp] [แล้ว|Láaeo][ก็|kâw][ขอ|khǎaw][กาแฟ|kaa-fae][หนึ่ง|nùeng][แก้ว|kâaeo][ด้วย|dûai][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: Big ones. And a cup of coffee too, please.
lines.literal: bottle — big — (polite). then — also — ask-for — coffee — one — glass — too — (polite).

lines.speaker: พนักงาน:
lines.text: [ร้อน|Ráwn][หรือ|rǔue][เย็น|yen][คะ|khá]

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [เย็น|Yen][ครับ|khráp] [มี|Mii][ขนมปัง|khà-nǒm-pang][ไหม|mǎi][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: Iced. Do you have any bread?

lines.speaker: พนักงาน:
lines.text: [มี|Mii][ค่ะ|khâ] [อยู่|Yùu][ตรง|trong][นั้น|nán][ค่ะ|khâ]

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [เอา|Ao][สาม|sǎam][ชิ้น|chín][ครับ|khráp] [แล้ว|Láaeo][ก็|kâw][ขอ|khǎaw][ถุง|thǔng][หนึ่ง|nùeng][ใบ|bai][ด้วย|dûai][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: I'll take three pieces. And a bag too, please.
lines.literal: take — three — piece — (polite). then — also — ask-for — bag — one — sheet — too — (polite).

lines.speaker: พนักงาน:
lines.text: [ถุง|Thǔng][ใบ|bai][ละ|lá][สอง|sǎawng][บาท|bàat][นะ|ná][คะ|khá]
lines.id: Bags are two baht each, okay?
lines.literal: bag — sheet — per — two — baht — okay — (polite)?

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [ไม่เป็นไร|Mâi pen rai][ครับ|khráp] [ทั้งหมด|Tháng-mòt][กี่|kìi][บาท|bàat][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: That's fine. How many baht altogether?

lines.speaker: พนักงาน:
lines.text: [แปด|Pàaet][สิบ|sìp][เจ็ด|jèt][บาท|bàat][ค่ะ|khâ] [รับ|Ráp][ถุง|thǔng][กี่|kìi][ใบ|bai][คะ|khá]
lines.id: Eighty-seven baht. How many bags would you like?
lines.literal: eight — ten — seven — baht — (polite). receive — bag — how-many — sheet — (polite)?

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [ใบ|Bai][เดียว|diao][ครับ|khráp] [พอ|Phaw][แล้ว|láaeo][ครับ|khráp]

notes: **The order is always: NOUN — NUMBER — CLASSIFIER.** *น้ำสองขวด* = water two bottle. *เสื้อสามตัว* = shirt three (body). English puts the number first ("two bottles of water"); Thai puts the thing first. Once that clicks, the rest follows.

**When the number is ONE, the order can flip** to **NOUN — CLASSIFIER — หนึ่ง**: *ถุงใบหนึ่ง* sounds more natural than *ถุงหนึ่งใบ*, though both are correct. Shorter still: **NOUN — CLASSIFIER — เดียว** (*diao*, single) means "just one": *ใบเดียว* = just one (bag).

**To point to a specific item, the classifier is required too**: **NOUN — CLASSIFIER — นี้/นั้น**. *เสื้อตัวนี้* = this shirt. *คนนั้น* = that person. ⚠️ This one often gets forgotten: "this shirt" isn't *เสื้อนี้* but *เสื้อ**ตัว**นี้*.

**กี่ kìi asks "how many", and it is ALWAYS followed by a classifier**, never on its own: *กี่คน* (how many people), *กี่ใบ* (how many bags/tickets), *กี่บาท* (how many baht). Compare *เท่าไหร่* from Unit 3, which is never followed by a classifier.
**ขอ khǎaw means "may I have" and is softer than เอา ao.** For small items and food, *ขอ…ครับ/ค่ะ* is the most comfortable form. Add *หน่อย nàwy* to make it gentler still: *ขอน้ำหน่อยครับ*.
**ด้วย dûai at the end means "too, as well" when asking for something extra.** *ขอถุงด้วยครับ* = a bag too, please. The same word also means "with" and "together".

**Some nouns serve as their own classifier.** *ห้องสองห้อง* (two rooms), *คนสามคน* (three people), *ประเทศห้าประเทศ* (five countries). If a noun sounds like a container or a unit, it's very likely its own classifier.

**พนักงาน phá-nák-ngaan means "staff member, employee"** — the general word for anyone serving you in a shop. To address them, Thais use *น้อง náwng* (younger sibling) if they're younger, or *พี่ phîi* (older sibling) if they're older. These terms are warm, not condescending.

grammars.title: Twelve classifiers that cover almost all A1 needs
body: Learn the first ten rows; the rest will come on their own through use.

head: Classifier
Pronunciation
For
Example
rows: นักเรียนสามคน — three students
หมาสองตัว — two dogs
containers & sheets: bags, tickets, empty glasses, documents
ตั๋วสองใบ — two tickets
เบียร์สามขวด — three bottles of beer
กาแฟหนึ่งแก้ว — a cup of coffee
ผัดไทยสองจาน — two plates of pad thai
เค้กสองชิ้น — two pieces of cake
ส้มห้าลูก — five oranges
หนังสือสองเล่ม — two books
รถหนึ่งคัน — one car
แอร์สองเครื่อง — two air conditioners
small things in general — and your safety net
อันนี้ — this one

after: ⚠️ **ใบ and แก้ว are often mixed up.** *แก้ว* is for a glass **of a drink** you order; *ใบ* is for a glass as an **empty object** you buy. Ordering *กาแฟหนึ่งใบ* sounds like you're buying the cup, not the coffee.
⚠️ **ตัว is used for both clothes and animals**, and that's no joke — the logic is "things with a body". Chairs and tables belong here too.

grammars.title: Three patterns that use classifiers

head: Purpose
Pattern
Example
rows: น้ำสองขวด — two bottles of water
noun + classifier + หนึ่ง / เดียว
ถุงใบหนึ่ง / ใบเดียว
noun + classifier + นี้ / นั้น / ไหน
เสื้อตัวนี้ — this shirt
คนกี่คน — how many people
ใบละสองบาท — two baht each

after: The fourth pattern, *…กี่…*, is the one you'll **hear** most: *กี่คนคะ* (how many people?) is the first thing a restaurant server says as you walk in the door.

blocks.text: It will happen, often, and it's no big deal. There are three ways out, and Thais will understand all of them.

blocks.title: Three ways out
items: **Use อัน *an*.** It's the general classifier for small things and works as a safety net. You'll sound foreign, but you'll always be understood.
**Repeat the noun as its own classifier.** *ขอกาแฟสองกาแฟ* is wrong, but people will still give you two coffees. Plenty of nouns really do work this way (ห้อง, คน, ประเทศ).
**Point and say just the number.** *สองครับ* while pointing at a bottle of water is enough, and that's what Thais do themselves when they're in a hurry.

blocks.text: What you **can't** skip is the classifier in the pointing pattern: *เสื้อนี้* sounds broken to a Thai ear, while *เสื้อตัวนี้* sounds natural. If you have to choose one place to be careful, choose this one.

blocks.title: น้ำ: one word, many faces
items: *น้ำ náam* means "water", but it also heads dozens of other words: *น้ำแข็ง náam-khǎeng* (ice — literally "hard water"), *น้ำผลไม้ náam-phǒn-lá-mái* (juice), *น้ำมัน náam-man* (oil — "oily water"), *น้ำหอม náam-hǎwm* (perfume — "fragrant water"), *น้ำตา náam-taa* (tears — "eye water"), *ห้องน้ำ hâwng-náam* (bathroom — "water room").
Mastering this one word unlocks dozens of others at once. It's a pattern that repeats across all of Thai: simple words are combined into new ones, rather than borrowed from foreign roots.

นักเรียนสาม____ (three students)
หนังสือสี่____ (four books)
เสื้อสอง____ (two shirts)
ตั๋วห้า____ (five tickets)
"This shirt" → เสื้อ____นี้
"How many people?" → ____คนคะ
"Two baht each" → ใบ____สองบาท
"Just one bag" → ถุงใบ____
"Some water too, please" → ขอน้ำ____ครับ
